name: Belarus
snapshot: Alexander Lukashenko has been trading political prisoners for US sanctions relief, while staying firmly in Russia's camp and hosting its nuclear weapons.
culture: Belarusian culture has long been overshadowed by Russian, and most people speak Russian day to day, though the white-red-white flag and the Belarusian language became symbols of the 2020 protest movement. The country lost about a quarter of its population in the Second World War, which remains central to state identity. Ice hockey is the president's favourite sport and a national passion.
society: Lukashenko crushed the 2020 protests after a stolen election, and hundreds of thousands left. More than a thousand political prisoners remained in 2025, though releases have since continued in deals with Washington. The economy relies heavily on Russian subsidies and markets. Belarus served as a launchpad for Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
situation: Alexander Lukashenko has ruled Belarus since 1994, longer than anyone in Europe. In 2020, after an election widely seen as stolen from opposition candidate Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, hundreds of thousands marched in Minsk. He crushed them with mass arrests and torture, survived with Russia's help, and later let Putin use Belarus to invade Ukraine. The West answered with sanctions. In 2026, Lukashenko found a way to sell his prisoners back.

Under Trump, a US envoy, John Coale, has made repeated trips to Minsk, trading prisoner releases for sanctions relief. On 19 March Lukashenko freed 250 political prisoners, the largest group yet, and Washington lifted sanctions on two state banks, the Finance Ministry and the big potash producers, whose fertiliser is Belarus's main export (AP via WTOP). Earlier deals had freed Nobel laureate Ales Bialiatski and opposition figures Maria Kolesnikova and Viktar Babaryka. Coale said he expected all political prisoners to be freed by year's end, in exchange for lifting all sanctions imposed after 2020 (Polskie Radio). But released prisoners are expelled to Lithuania without passports, and the regime keeps arresting new people: by September, after another release of 25, the rights group Viasna still counted 887 political prisoners (AP via MyNorthwest). Critics call it a revolving door: hostages taken and sold for concessions. Europe has kept its own sanctions in place.
power: A personalist dictatorship. The president controls the security services, courts and media; parliament and elections are managed. Russian nuclear weapons have been stationed in Belarus since 2023 under a union-state treaty.
holders: President Alexander Lukashenko, since 1994, re-elected in January 2025.
